The correct answer is D  The innate immune system is comprised of the cells in the blood and in the tissues.  In the blood you will find basophils, eosinophils, neutrophils, and monocytes. In the tissues you will find dendritic cells, macrophages, mast cells, and natural killer cells.  The innate immune system is the first line of defence against pathogens and is not very specific.  The cells in the blood travel to the site of infection and the cells in the tissue are already present.  The cells in the blood are propelled to the site of infection by chemotaxis - movement in response to a chemical stimulus.  The cells in the tissue recognise the chemical stimulus and release chemicals that cause the blood cells to move towards the site of infection.  The cells in the blood are propelled by receptors on their surface that bind to the chemicals released by the tissue cells.  Once at the site of infection the cells in the blood can then phagocytose - engulf and destroy - pathogens.  The cells in the tissue can also phagocytose pathogens and the cells in the blood can also stimulate the tissue cells to do so.  The cells in the blood can also release chemicals that cause the tissue cells to become more phagocytic.  The cells in the blood can also release chemicals that cause the tissue cells to release inflammatory cytokines.  The inflammatory cytokines cause vasodilation of nearby blood vessels which causes more cells from the blood to be propelled to the site of infection.

Calsequestrin is the correct answer. It is a Ca2+ binding protein that keeps Ca2+ locked in the SR. Increased Ca2+ in the cell (ie. via L-type Ca2+ channels during a cardiac action potential) removes this effect and causes calcium-induced-calcium release.  Calbindin is a Ca2+ binding protein that is found in smooth muscle cells. It binds Ca2+ and allows the Ca2+ to stay in the cell for a longer period of time. This is important in smooth muscle as it has no mitochondria and cannot pump the Ca2+ back out of the cell. Calmodulin is a Ca2+ binding protein that is found in smooth muscle cells. It binds Ca2+ and activates MLCK (which phosphorylates myosin light chain) and contributes to contraction. Phospholamban is a Ca2+ pump inhibitor. It inhibits SERCA (which pumps Ca2+ into the SR) and also pumps Ca2+ out of the cell. It is phosphorylated by PKA and this removes its inhibitory effect. This is important in SA node cells as it allows the SR to fill up quickly and so the heart to contract quickly. SERCA is a Ca2+ pump that pumps Ca2+ into the SR. It is the main mechanism of Ca2+ storage in non-excitable cells.

Amiodarone is known to prolong the action potential so is the most likely cause of the torsade de Pointes.  All of these drugs are rate and rhythm control drugs but amiodarone is the only one that affects the action potential.  Torsade de Pointes is a polymorphic ventricular tachycardia which is characterised by a characteristic undulating pattern on a ECG. The PaO2 value tells us that this patient is still hypoxaemic on 40% O2, which is bad given his history of COPD. The pH is normal so we know that there is no primary acidosis or alkalosis. The PaCO2 is low (normal 4.7-6.0) which tells us that there is no respiratory alkalosis. The PaCO2 is high (normal 4.7-6.0) which tells us that there is respiratory acidosis. The HCO3- is high (normal 22-26) which tells us that there is metabolic alkalosis. Therefore, the patient has respiratory acidosis compensated by metabolic alkalosis. This is a common picture in COPD patients on chronic hypercapnia, where the body compensates by retaining HCO3- and excreting H+ in order to normalise the pH.
